Relics

Abandoned but not forgotten.

Every time we reach for another world, something gets left behind. A robot that tested the Moon’s ground. A rover that kept driving until the dust won. A helicopter built for five flights that flew seventy-two. We call them abandoned. We haven’t forgotten a single one. Come and meet them.

Enter the world of relics

The Moon

The Moon has no wind or rain to wear things away. Here are four stories, in the order they happened. They begin with a robot sent to answer one question: will the ground hold? Tap a card to open it.

Dates and times are in Universal Time (UT), the way NASA’s archives record them.

Before anyone dared to stand on the Moon, a robot went first to check the floor.

Nobody knew if the Moon’s surface would hold up a spaceship. It might be solid rock. It might be deep dust that would swallow a lander whole. So in April 1967, Surveyor 3 went to find out, and the landing was a mess. Bright rocks fooled its landing radar, its engine kept burning when it should have stopped, and the little lander bounced twice, about 10 metres up and then about 3 metres, before it finally settled on the third touchdown.

It did not give up. Its scoop arm dug four trenches and ran four bearing tests and thirteen impact tests, and its camera sent home 6,326 pictures. The answer was good news for everyone waiting to follow: the soil behaves like wet sand, and it is strong enough to carry a lunar module. On 4 May 1967, two days into the freezing lunar night, Surveyor 3 made its last contact.

But the story had a second chapter. In November 1969, Apollo 12 landed about 180 metres away. Two astronauts walked over to the robot that had tested the ground for them, took parts of it, including the soil scoop and the camera system, and carried them home so scientists could see what two and a half years on the Moon had done to metal and wire.

Launched
17 April 1967
Landed
20 April 1967
Where
Oceanus Procellarum, about 3° S, 23.41° W
Mass
997.9 kg (2,200 lb)
Pictures sent
6,326
Last contact
4 May 1967

Where it is now: still on the Moon where it landed, minus the parts that came home with Apollo 12.

The first footsteps on the Moon came with a quiet promise: we came in peace.

On 20 July 1969, Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin set Eagle down in the Sea of Tranquility. Armstrong radioed, “Houston, Tranquility Base here. The Eagle has landed.” Eagle was really two machines stacked together. The top half, the ascent stage, carried the astronauts back up to their ship in orbit. The bottom half, the descent stage, was their launch pad, and it stayed behind.

They left more than a launch pad. A small science kit called EASEP, with a seismometer and a dust detector, ran on two solar panels, so it could only work in daylight. It ran 30 °C hotter than planned and still worked. It was switched off before the first lunar night, woken up for a second day, and on 27 August 1969 it stopped accepting commands from Earth. Before climbing back in, Armstrong also left a packet of memorial items on the ground.

A laser reflector sits about 5 metres from the science kit. It needs no power at all, so it never had to be switched off. The ascent stage was released into lunar orbit on 22 July, and nobody knows exactly what became of it. NASA assumes it crashed into the Moon within one to four months.

“Here men from the planet Earth first set foot upon the Moon July 1969, A.D. We came in peace for all mankind.”

The plaque fixed to Eagle’s descent stage, read aloud by the crew
Landed
20 July 1969, 20:17 UT
Where

Time on the surface

About 250 m

Where it is now: the descent stage, the science kit and the laser reflector are still at the landing site. The ascent stage’s fate is unknown.

Two astronauts landed so close to an old robot that they could walk over and visit it.

On 19 November 1969, Pete Conrad and Alan Bean landed Intrepid in the Ocean of Storms (Oceanus Procellarum), so close to Surveyor 3 that they could walk to it. It was about 180 metres away. On their second moonwalk they did exactly that, and brought back about 10 kg of its parts.

Not everything went to plan. Early on, the TV camera was pointed at the Sun by accident and damaged, so the live pictures stopped. The crew carried on anyway. Across two moonwalks totalling 7 hours 45 minutes they walked 1.35 km and collected 34.35 kg of rock and soil.

They also left a science station called ALSEP, with six instruments including a seismometer, a magnetometer and a dust detector. It ran on a small nuclear generator fuelled with about 4 kg of plutonium-238 and was switched on the day they landed. NASA shut it down, along with the other Apollo stations, on 30 September 1977.

Intrepid’s ascent stage had one last job. After the crew docked with the orbiting spacecraft, it was sent crashing into the Moon on purpose, about 72 km from the seismic station. It made the first recorded artificial moonquake.

Landed
19 November 1969, 06:54 UT
Where
Oceanus Procellarum, 3.013° S, 23.422° W
Distance to Surveyor 3

Where it is now: the descent stage and the science station are still at the landing site. The ascent stage crashed about 72 km away.

A hammer, a feather, and a quiet promise to the people who never made it home.

Apollo 15 landed at the foot of the Apennine mountains, beside a long channel called Hadley Rille. David Scott and James Irwin were the first crew to drive a rover on the Moon. Over three moonwalks totalling 18 hours 35 minutes they covered 27.9 km, never more than about 5 km from the lander, and collected 77.31 kg of rock and soil.

At the end, Scott held up a hammer and a feather for the cameras and let go. They landed at the same time, because there is no air on the Moon to slow the feather.

Then came a quieter moment. The astronauts left a small plaque and a figure on the surface in memory of the fourteen American and Soviet space explorers who had died by then. Two nations that had been rivals were remembered side by side, far from home.

Falcon left more behind: a science station with seven instruments, powered by a nuclear generator with about 4 kg of plutonium-238. It was switched on 31 July 1971 and shut down by command on 30 September 1977. The top half of Falcon did one last job. After bringing the crew to the orbiting ship, it was released on 3 August and hit the Moon about two hours later.

Landed
30 July 1971, 22:16 UT
Where
Foot of the Apennines, 26.132° N, 3.633° E
Time on the Moon
66 hours 55 minutes
Moonwalks
3, totalling 18 hours 35 minutes
Distance driven
27.9 km
Samples collected
77.31 kg

Where it is now: the descent stage, the science station, the plaque and the figure are still at the landing site. The ascent stage hit the Moon about two hours after it was released.

Mars

Mars is far enough away that every machine we send is on a one-way trip. These five made it to the surface and worked there. Each story ends with the last signal we know of.

The first machine to land on Mars and keep working, silenced by a single wrong command.

People had tried before. A Soviet lander, Mars 3, touched down in 1971 but went silent seconds later. Then, in 1976, Viking 1 arrived. Its orbiter scouted the planned landing site first and found it rougher than expected, so the team picked a new spot on the western slopes of Chryse Planitia. Viking 1 landed about 28 km from its planned target.

Minutes later it took the first photograph ever taken on the surface of Mars. On 28 July its robot arm scooped up soil for experiments designed to look for life. The answers were unclear: a weak positive from some of the tests, and a negative from the main test for organic compounds.

Viking 1 kept sending weather reports for years. In January 1982 it was renamed the Thomas Mutch Memorial Station, after the leader of the imaging team who had died in 1980.

Silent for …

Last signal

11 November 1982. A faulty command sent from Earth interrupted communications, and every attempt to reconnect failed. The orbiter had gone quiet earlier, on 7 August 1980, after it ran out of the fuel it used to keep itself pointed.

Launched
20 August 1975
Landed
20 July 1976
Where
Chryse Planitia, 22.48° N, 47.94° W
Lander mass
978 kg
Power
Two nuclear generators
Pictures, both Viking missions
52,663 from orbit, 4,500 from the ground

Where it is now: still at Chryse Planitia.

It arrived on Mars like a beach ball and carried a tiny rover with a big name.

Pathfinder arrived like a beach ball. It fell through the thin air on a parachute, inflated giant airbags about 100 metres above the ground, and bounced about 15 times, as high as 15 metres, before it rolled to a stop 2.5 minutes later, roughly 1 km from where it first hit.

Inside was Sojourner, a rover about 30 centimetres tall and weighing 10.6 kg, named after Sojourner Truth. On the night of 5 July it rolled down a ramp onto Mars. The lander that carried it was named the Carl Sagan Memorial Station, after the astronomer who had died the year before.

Pathfinder began as a technology test, a way to find out whether this clever, low-cost idea would even work. It worked. It sent back 2.3 billion bits of data, more than 16,500 images from the lander, 550 from the rover and more than 15 chemical analyses of rocks and soil. Rounded pebbles at its landing site, an ancient flood plain called Ares Vallis, suggested that water once flowed there.

Silent for …

Last signal

27 September 1997. The final data transmission came about three months after landing.

Landed
4 July 1997
Where
Ares Vallis, an ancient flood plain
Landing speed
14 m/s (31 mph), cushioned by airbags
Rover
Sojourner, 10.6 kg
Data returned

Final transmission

Where it is now: still at Ares Vallis.

Two identical twins, sent to opposite sides of Mars to answer one question: was there once water?

They were launched as a pair and landed in January 2004. Spirit touched down in Gusev Crater, a possible ancient lake. Opportunity landed on Meridiani Planum, where mineral deposits hinted at a wet past. Between them, they confirmed that water once stood on the surface for a long time.

Spirit’s story ended in the cold. It drove 7.7 km. After a Martian winter with little sunlight, it probably had too little energy to run its survival heaters. NASA’s last communication from Spirit was on 22 March 2010, and the attempts to reach it ended in May 2011.

Opportunity’s story ended in the dark. It drove 45.16 km, the distance record for any vehicle on another world. Then a planet-wide dust storm covered its solar panels, and its last communication came on 10 June 2018. Engineers sent more than a thousand commands trying to wake it before NASA ended the mission on 13 February 2019, after nearly 15 years.

That record stood until 11 October 2026, when Perseverance passed it. Opportunity’s 45.16 km is the number its successor had to beat.

Spirit silent for …Opportunity silent for …

What were Opportunity’s last words?

You may have seen “My battery is low and it’s getting dark” called its final message. It wasn’t. A reporter wrote that line as his own plain-English reading of the final transmission, and people shared it as if the rover had said it. The real last transmission was a short burst of data showing that power was low as the dust storm closed in.

Spirit landed
January 2004, Gusev Crater
Opportunity landed
January 2004, Meridiani Planum
Spirit drove
7.7 km
Opportunity drove
45.16 km
Spirit last heard
22 March 2010
Opportunity last heard
10 June 2018

Where they are now: Spirit is still in Gusev Crater and Opportunity is still on Meridiani Planum.

It listened to the heartbeat of another planet, and then it said goodbye in its own voice.

InSight was not built to study the surface. It was built to measure the inside of Mars: its pulse, its temperature, its reflexes. Its robotic arm, 1.8 metres long, lifted a seismometer and a heat probe off the deck and set them gently on the ground.

It landed on Elysium Planitia, a flat plain near the equator chosen because it was safe, about 600 km from where Curiosity landed. On 1 December 2018 its sensors picked up a low rumble made by the Martian wind, blowing at about 5 to 7 metres a second.

Over the next four years dust slowly built up on its solar panels until there was not enough power left to keep going. Its last messages came from the lander’s official social media account, posted in the lander’s own voice.

“Don’t worry about me though: my time here has been both productive and serene.”

“Thanks for staying with me.”

From InSight’s final messages
Silent for …

Last signal

NASA lists the end of the mission as 15 December 2022. After the lander missed two scheduled contacts, NASA declared the mission over on 21 December 2022.

Landed

Where it is now: still on Elysium Planitia.

It was only supposed to fly five times. It flew seventy-two.

Ingenuity rode to Mars strapped under the Perseverance rover. It was a technology test that was supposed to make no more than five flights in 30 days. On 19 April 2021 it made the first powered, controlled flight on another planet.

Then it just kept going. It flew 72 times over nearly three years: about 128.8 minutes in the air, 17 km covered, up to 24 metres high and as fast as 10 metres a second. Along the way it scouted ahead for Perseverance and helped engineers learn more about debris from Perseverance’s landing gear.

On its 72nd flight, on 18 January 2024, Ingenuity climbed to about 12 metres, hovered for a few seconds and came back down. It lost contact with Perseverance, the rover that relayed its messages, while about 1 metre above the ground. When contact returned, pictures showed that one or more rotor blades had been damaged in the landing. Damaged blades cannot lift a helicopter, so it could not fly again, and NASA ended the mission on 25 January 2024.

“That remarkable helicopter flew higher and farther than we ever imagined.”

NASA Administrator Bill Nelson, on the end of the mission
Launched
30 July 2020, with Perseverance
Reached Jezero Crater
18 February 2021
Flights

Time in the air
About 128.8 minutes
Distance flown
17 km
Highest flight

Where it is now: in Jezero Crater, where it last landed.

Mars isn’t finished with us

Perseverance is still driving. It passed Opportunity’s distance record on 11 October 2026. NASA’s SkyFall mission, announced on 24 March 2026, builds on Ingenuity: a team of next-generation Mars helicopters, released in mid-air, to scout human landing sites and map subsurface water ice. In March tests, the rotor blades meant for those helicopters broke the sound barrier.

Deep Space

Past Mars there is no ground to leave footprints on. These machines went where there is only dark, distance and silence. One rests on an asteroid. One circles a dwarf planet. One watches from its own orbit around the Sun. One is still drifting out of the solar system. Several of them did far more than anyone planned, and every one of them is a very long way from home.

It was built to last 21 months, and it kept whispering back for more than thirty years.

In 1972, Pioneer 10 set out to do something nobody had done: cross the asteroid belt and reach the outer planets. It did it. It became the first spacecraft to fly through the asteroid belt, the first to fly past Jupiter and the first to cross Neptune’s orbit. On 4 December 1973 it raced past Jupiter, 130,354 km away, and sent home about 500 pictures of the giant planet.

It was designed for a mission of 21 months. It kept going for decades. NASA stayed in routine contact for more than two decades, until 31 March 1997, when routine contact ended for budget reasons. Even then, weak signals kept arriving for years, like a friend waving from far away.

And it carries a message. Fixed to its side is an aluminum plaque showing a man and a woman, the solar system and the Sun’s position relative to 14 pulsars, in case anyone ever finds it. Pioneer 10 is heading roughly toward the red star Aldebaran and should pass it in about two million years.

Two million years from now, long after everyone who built it is gone, it will still be out there, carrying a hello.

Silent for …

Last signal

23 January 2003, from 12.23 billion km away. The signal took 11 hours 20 minutes to reach Earth. By then the spacecraft’s nuclear power source had faded too far to run its radio. One more attempt, in March 2006, got no answer.

Launched
2 March 1972
Closest to Jupiter
4 December 1973, 130,354 km
Crossed Neptune’s orbit
13 June 1983
Routine contact ended
31 March 1997
Mass
258 kg
Last signal
23 January 2003

Where it is now: drifting out of the solar system, heading toward Aldebaran.

It was never meant to land. It landed anyway, and it kept whispering for two more weeks.

NEAR Shoemaker was a first in two ways: the first spacecraft to orbit an asteroid, and the first to land on one. The trip started badly. An aborted engine burn in December 1998 meant it reached the asteroid Eros about a year late. On 14 February 2000 it finally entered orbit, and it spent a year circling Eros, a lumpy world about 34 km (21 miles) long, mapping more than 70 percent of its surface.

Then the team tried something bold. On 12 February 2001 NEAR made a slow, controlled descent, taking 69 close-up photos on the way down, and touched down at about 6.4 km/h near a saddle-shaped feature named Himeros. NEAR was never designed to land.

It survived anyway. It kept sending data, especially from its gamma-ray spectrometer, for about two weeks, a bonus nobody had planned for. The spacecraft was renamed in honour of the geologist Eugene Shoemaker, and over its life it returned about 10 times more data than planned, including 160,000 images.

Silent for …

Last signal

28 February 2001. The cold, about minus 173 °C, silenced it. NASA tried again in December 2002 and got no reply.

Launched
17 February 1996
Entered orbit
14 February 2000
Landed
12 February 2001
Eros is about
34 km (21 miles) long
Images returned
160,000
Last contact

Where it is now: on Eros, where it landed.

It stayed at two different worlds, and it will keep circling the second one for decades.

Dawn was NASA’s first truly interplanetary spaceship, built for long stays instead of quick flybys. Its two destinations were in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter: Vesta, a giant asteroid, and Ceres, a dwarf planet. It reached Vesta in 2011 and Ceres in 2015, and at each one it settled into orbit to study the world up close.

Its long trip was powered by an ion engine, a thruster that glows blue and pushes very gently, for a very long time.

On 1 November 2018, NASA announced that Dawn had run out of hydrazine, the fuel for the thrusters that point it. Without them it could not aim its antenna at Earth, point its instruments at Ceres or turn its solar panels toward the Sun.

NASA says Dawn will stay in orbit around Ceres for at least 20 years, and probably much longer. It will keep circling, silent, around the world it travelled so far to meet.

Last signal

Check-ins scheduled for 31 October and 1 November 2018 never arrived, and NASA announced the end of the mission on 1 November.

Launched
27 September 2007
Visited
Vesta and Ceres
Ran out of fuel
Announced 1 November 2018
Orbit
Around Ceres, for at least 20 years

Where it is now: in orbit around Ceres.

It stared at one tiny patch of sky and showed us that planets are everywhere.

Kepler’s whole job was to watch for a shadow. It stared at about 150,000 stars in one patch of sky, waiting for the tiny dip in brightness when a planet crosses in front of a star. In its first six weeks it found five planets.

Then things went wrong. In May 2013 the second of its four reaction wheels failed. Without a third wheel it could not hold still, because sunlight itself pushes on the spacecraft. Engineers had a clever fix: use the pressure of sunlight to steady the telescope, like a kayak steering into a current. The new mission, called K2, was expected to manage 10 observing campaigns on the fuel it had left. It managed 19.

On 30 October 2018 NASA retired Kepler, out of the fuel it needed for science, and left it in a safe orbit away from Earth. It leaves behind more than 2,600 planet discoveries, and a changed view of the sky.

“When we started conceiving this mission 35 years ago, we didn’t know of a single planet outside our solar system.”

“Now that we know planets are everywhere, Kepler has set us on a new course that’s full of promise for future generations to explore our galaxy.”

William Borucki, Kepler’s founding principal investigator
Launched
6 March 2009
Second wheel failed
May 2013
K2 campaigns
19, from a plan of 10
Retired
30 October 2018
Planets found
More than 2,600
Stars surveyed, Kepler and K2
More than 500,000

Where it is now: in orbit around the Sun, away from Earth.

Still out there.

Most of these machines will never come home. Some went quiet in the cold, some under the dust, and one was switched off to save money. Each one taught us something. Their names, dates and last signals are written down here so they stay remembered.
